54:4.text: And it came to pass in the morning, that David wrote a letter to Joab, and sent it by the hand of Uriah.

provenance.other: “and sent it by” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 2 Samuel 11:14, and “sent it by the hand” in exactly one, the same verse. “wrote a letter” occurs in exactly four (2 Samuel 11:14, 2 Kings 10:6, Ezra 4:8, Acts 23:25), and 2 Samuel 11:14 is the only one of them that also has the sending clause.
provenance.significance: The KJV's one letter sent by a named bearer is the letter David wrote to Joab and sent by the hand of Uriah — a document carried by the man it condemns to death, who cannot read it. Alma 54:4 sends its epistle 'by the servant of Ammoron, the same who had brought an epistle to Moroni', and the epistle it carries is a refusal to trade prisoners except at a price its bearer's master will not pay, closing with the sentence that he is a child of hell. The correspondence in this chapter runs on messengers who carry threats against their own side, and the wording comes from the Bible's one instance of the practice at its worst. Compare Hays on metalepsis: the borrowed clause is unremarkable until the recovered context supplies what the Book of Mormon does not say, namely that a letter of this kind is a way of killing a man by the hand that holds it.

54:4.note: 'Therefore he wrote an epistle, and sent it by the servant of Ammoron, the same who had brought an epistle to Moroni.' A KJV singleton on four words, and the surrounding sentence reproduces the source's whole action — wrote, and sent it by, plus a named bearer belonging to the other party. The n-gram stream ranked it first for the verse and was right. Below Skousen's sixteen-word threshold and not one of his 36.

54:11.text: Woe unto you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! for ye compass sea and land to make one proselyte, and when he is made, ye make him twofold more the child of hell than yourselves.

provenance.other: “child of hell” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Matthew 23:15. The catalogue adjudicates the borrowing at Alma 11:23, where Amulek says 'O thou child of Hell' to Zeezrom and the 1830 capitalizes the noun; the argument for the dependence is made there and is not repeated here.
provenance.significance: This is not the Alma 11 formula recurring — it is the other half of the same verse being used. At 11:23 what mattered was the speaker: the phrase is Jesus's, from the week of the Jerusalem confrontation, and Amulek takes it up in a confrontation of the same shape. Here what matters is the syntax of Matthew's insult, which is about manufacture. A child of hell in Matthew 23:15 is not born but made — 'ye compass sea and land to make one proselyte, and when he is made, ye make him twofold more the child of hell than yourselves' — and Ammoron is the Book of Mormon's most exact instance of the type. He is a Nephite by descent who says so himself twelve verses later ('I am Ammoron, and a descendant of Zoram'), converted into a Lamanite king by his brother's proselytizing, and more violent in the office than the people who made him. Moroni calls him what Jesus calls a convert who has outdone his converters.

54:11.note: 'It supposeth me that thou art a child of hell.' A KJV singleton, and its second use in this book. It is written as a link rather than registered as a repeat because the second use turns on a feature of the source the first did not touch: Matthew's child of hell is a made proselyte, and Ammoron's whole identity in this chapter is that he was made into what he is and has exceeded his makers, which he half-admits at 54:23-24. CONVENTIONS §4's default sends a within-book repeat to the register; the exception for a phrase that goes back to work on its source is what is claimed here.

54:11.text: Then answered all the wicked men and men of Belial, of those that went with David, and said, Because they went not with us, we will not give them ought of the spoil that we have recovered, save to every man his wife and his children, that they may lead them away, and depart.

provenance.route: 1 Samuel 30:22 (with 1 Samuel 30:1-3, 18-19) → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “his wife and his children” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 1 Samuel 30:22. The catalogue's usual caution about a family formula does not apply: the KJV's ordinary phrasings are 'his wives and his children', 'their wives and their children', 'thy sons and thy daughters', and the exact singular-plus-plural string Alma 54:11 uses stands in one verse only.
provenance.significance: The verse the phrase comes from is the Bible's one negotiation about returning captured non-combatants. At Ziklag the Amalekites carry off the wives and children and burn the city; David recovers everything, 'and David rescued his two wives'; and then the men of Belial in his own force propose that those who did not fight should get nothing back of the spoil 'save to every man his wife and his children' — that is, that a wife and children are the minimum a man is owed and everything else is negotiable. Alma 54:11 sets the identical unit and inverts the arithmetic: 'ye will deliver up a man, and his wife, and his children, for one prisoner.' Moroni prices a whole family against a single soldier because the Lamanites hold Nephite women and children and he holds none (54:3), which is exactly the asymmetry 1 Samuel 30 is about. The chapter's harshest sentence is built out of the KJV's one verse on the recovery of captive families, and it is spoken by the party the source assigns to the men of Belial.

54:11.note: 'Save it be on conditions that ye will deliver up a man, and his wife, and his children, for one prisoner.' A KJV singleton whose verse is not merely rare but situationally identical — captured wives and children, a recovery, and a hard bargain over what the non-combatants are worth. The machine ranked 1 Samuel 30:22 second for this verse on the shared words and had no way to see the situational agreement, which is what raises the row to high.

54:12.text: And if any mischief follow, then thou shalt give life for life,

provenance.other: “life for life” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Exodus 21:23. Deuteronomy 19:21 has 'life shall go for life' and Leviticus 24:18 'beast for beast', so the bare formula is Exodus's alone. “blood for blood” occurs in no KJV verse at all — the Book of Mormon has coined a member for the series that the Bible does not have. The Sermon on the Mount quotes the talionic list at Matthew 5:38 and drops the life clause entirely, keeping only 'An eye for an eye, and a tooth for a tooth'; `mediation-check.py` returns two decisive points for Exodus 21:23 over Matthew 5:38 on that ground, so the mediation is direct-OT.
provenance.alternative: 1 Kings 20:42 is the other candidate and is worth naming: 'thy life shall go for his life, and thy people for his people', said to Ahab for sparing a captured enemy king, and the same verse contains 'utter destruction', which Alma 54:9 has used three verses earlier. But the string Alma reproduces is Exodus's, not 1 Kings's.
provenance.significance: Moroni is writing about a prisoner exchange, which is the one context in which the lex talionis becomes an exchange rate rather than a punishment. Exodus 21:23 sets the price of a life at a life in a case of accidental injury to a pregnant woman — the KJV's most domestic application of the principle — and Moroni applies it to a war in which he has just demanded a man, his wife and his children for one soldier. The added 'blood for blood', which no KJV verse says, is the tell: he wants the Mosaic formula and then wants more than it gives, and the extra term is placed first.

54:12.note: 'Yea, and it shall be blood for blood; yea, life for life.' Three words from the KJV's only verse containing them, in the sentence of Moroni's epistle that states his terms. Catalogued as a quotation on the strength of the absolute rarity and the fact that the clause is reproduced whole, though it is three words and far below Skousen's sixteen-word threshold; it is not one of his 36. The mediation is a clean result rather than a default — the Gospel form of the talion has no life clause to borrow.

54:19.text: And Saul, yet breathing out threatenings and slaughter against the disciples of the Lord, went unto the high priest,

provenance.route: Acts 9:1, with Acts 4:29 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “breathing out threatenings” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Acts 9:1, and “threatenings” in exactly two, Acts 9:1 and Acts 4:29. The noun is confined to Acts. The 1830 spells it 'threatnings' at all three occurrences in this chapter (54:16 twice at 54:19), which is the same syncopated spelling the first edition uses at 1 Nephi 18:17; 1920 restored the KJV's 'threatenings'. The catalogue adjudicates the borrowing at 1 Nephi 18:17, and this row is written rather than registered because Alma is a different book and a different hand (CONVENTIONS §4, ratified 2026-09-05).
provenance.significance: Both Acts verses are in play and they belong to the two sides of this exchange. Ammoron accuses Moroni of the thing Saul of Tarsus is doing on the road to Damascus — 'ye have breathed out many threatnings against me and my people' — and answers it, twice, with the words of the disciples who were on the receiving end of exactly those threatenings: Acts 4:29's prayer is 'behold their threatenings: and grant unto thy servants, that with all boldness they may speak thy word', and Ammoron says 'we fear not your threatnings' at 54:16 and again at 54:19. So a Lamanite king denying that God exists is given the persecuted church's line, and the man he calls a persecutor is Moroni. Recover Acts 9 a verse or two further and the borrowing carries what neither correspondent wants: the KJV's one breather-out of threatenings is stopped on the road and becomes an apostle, which is what the whole epistolary exchange of Alma 54 refuses to imagine for anyone in it.

54:19.note: 'Behold, ye have breathed out many threatnings against me and my people; but behold, we fear not your threatnings.' A KJV singleton and a two-verse noun, both from Acts, in one sentence of Ammoron's reply. The argument for dependence was made at 1 Nephi 18:17, where Laman and Lemuel breathe out threatenings; it is given again here because Alma is a new book and a reader of this chapter shown nothing would be told there is no borrowing. What is new is the pairing with Acts 4:29 — the accusation and the retort come from the two sides of the same persecution — and the 1830 spelling, which preserves the KJV contact more plainly than the modern text does.

54:21.text: But I have understanding as well as you; I am not inferior to you: yea, who knoweth not such things as these?

provenance.route: Job 12:3 (the retort) + Acts 13:34 (the opening formula) → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “as well as you” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Job 12:3. “as concerning that” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Acts 13:34. Alma 54:21 opens with the second and closes with the first, and both were proposed independently by the n-gram stream for this verse.
provenance.significance: Job 12:3 is the Bible's sharpest sentence of a man refusing to be lectured about God — 'I have understanding as well as you; I am not inferior to you: yea, who knoweth not such things as these?' — spoken by Job to friends who have been explaining the deity to him. Ammoron's reply is the same speech-act by a man who has just been sent a lecture on the justice of God and the sword of his Almighty wrath, and it lands on the same words: 'we know not such a being; neither do ye … we know not but that he hath made us as well as you.' The difference is the one that makes the borrowing interesting. Job's retort is a believer's; he is claiming equal standing in a dispute about a God he does not doubt. Ammoron takes the same posture and empties it, arguing not that he knows God as well as Moroni does but that neither of them knows anything. The KJV formula that carries the opening is Acts 13:34's, the only 'as concerning that' in the Bible, and it introduces the resurrection — 'as concerning that he raised him up from the dead'. Ammoron's introduces his denial of a hereafter, which he completes at 54:22.

54:21.note: 'And as concerning that God whom ye say we have rejected, behold, we know not such a being; neither do ye; but if it so be that there is such a being, we know not but that he hath made us as well as you.' Two KJV singletons bracket the verse, one at each end, and neither is doing decorative work: the Acts formula frames a proposition about God's action and the Job formula asserts parity in a quarrel about God. Held at moderate rather than high because each singleton is short and the two come from unrelated books, so a reader may prefer to treat the coincidence as the ordinary King James colouring of the whole epistle.
54:21.whyNot: Four words and three words, from an OT wisdom dialogue and a Pauline sermon that have nothing to do with each other or with a war. 'As well as you' and 'as concerning that' are rare in the KJV largely because the KJV rarely needs them, not because they are marked phrases.
